# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This is the online edition of **Practical Approach to Learning Bioinformatics**.

Bioinformatics is learned the way laboratory work is learned: by doing it, making
mistakes, and developing judgement about what the results mean. This book is built
on that assumption. Every method it describes is demonstrated on data you can
download, with code you can run, producing output that is shown exactly as it was
produced. Nothing in these pages is illustrated with results that were never
computed.

The book takes you from the first command you type in a terminal to a complete,
reproducible analysis written up to the standard a journal would expect. Along the
way it covers the archives where biological data lives, the algorithms that compare
sequences, the Unix, Python and R skills that make large files tractable, the
analysis of genomes and sequencing reads, protein structure, biological networks,
statistics and machine learning for omics data, the clinical and public-health
applications of all of it, and the ethical obligations that come with working on
human genomes.

## How to read this book {.unnumbered}

If you are new to the field, read Chapters 1 and 2, then work through Part 4 (the
toolchain) before going further; the later chapters assume you can move around a
filesystem and read code. If you already program, you can start at Chapter 3 and
treat Part 4 as reference. The front matter chapter *How to use this book* explains
the conventions, how to install the software and how to get the data.

## Reproducing everything in the book {.unnumbered}

```bash
git clone https://github.com/babasaraki/practical-bioinformatics
cd practical-bioinformatics
conda env create -f environment.yml && conda activate pablb
python scripts/fetch_data.py       # ~12 MB of example data from public archives
quarto render                      # rebuilds the whole book
```

Every dataset used in the book is listed in `data/MANIFEST.tsv` with its source
archive, accession and SHA-256 checksum, so you can confirm that the files you have
are the files the book was written against.
